title: MAKE THE BELIEF BET
name: MAKE THE BELIEF BET
goal: Test a belief with a small action that could prove it wrong.
steps:
1. State the belief as a clear prediction.
2. Choose a safe, small action that could prove it wrong as well as right.
3. Picture the expected result before acting.
4. Run the test, then compare observation with prediction.
5. Pay out only to evidence.

title: THE EFFORT STAIRCASE
name: THE EFFORT STAIRCASE
goal: Start at the smallest task level that still leaves real evidence.
steps:
1. Name five versions of the task from almost easy to genuinely stretching.
2. Mentally remove the zero-effort decoy.
3. Do the smallest remaining version that leaves visible evidence—one paragraph, one call, one plate washed.
4. Next time, climb only one stair.

title: MOOD HAS ALIBIS
name: MOOD HAS ALIBIS
goal: Compare predicted mood with what actually changes during real activities.
steps:
1. Choose one activity.
2. Before it, score expected mood; at the start, notice your actual mood; at the end, score again.
3. Add one sentence about what changed during the activity.
4. Repeat with three different actions before deciding ‘nothing helps.’
numberedSteps:

3. Add one sentence about what changed during the activity.
4. Repeat with three different actions before deciding ‘nothing helps.’

title: TWO ENGINES
name: TWO ENGINES
goal: Feed pleasure and mastery separately instead of asking one activity to fix everything.
steps:
1. For the next day, schedule one act chosen purely for enjoyment and one chosen for competence.
2. Make both small enough to happen.
3. After each activity, ask which engine it fed: pleasure or mastery. Rate that one channel only.
4. Do not demand that either activity fix everything.
numberedSteps:
1. For the next day, schedule one act chosen purely for enjoyment and one chosen for competence.
2. Make both small enough to happen.
3. After each activity, ask which engine it fed: pleasure or mastery. Rate that one channel only.
4. Do not demand that either activity fix everything.
numbered_steps:

2. Make both small enough to happen.
3. After each activity, ask which engine it fed: pleasure or mastery. Rate that one channel only.
4. Do not demand that either activity fix everything.
win: One small enjoyable act and one competence-building act each delivered evidence to their own channel.

title: LET THE URGE MISS ITS APPOINTMENT
name: LET THE URGE MISS ITS APPOINTMENT

goal: Let an urge rise and fall without doing the usual ritual.
steps:

goal: Break the automatic reach by putting your body in a deliberate opposite position.
steps:

4. Then decide consciously.

full_consumer_ritual:
PLAY TIME
about 1 minute

GOAL
Break the automatic reach by putting your body in a deliberate opposite position.

STEPS
1. Spot the first motor cue—reaching, picking, scrolling, biting, clenching.
2. Use a safe opposite posture and practise it slowly three times.
3. When the cue appears, enter that posture for ten seconds while naming the urge.
4. Then decide consciously.

WIN
The first motor cue appeared, and your body paused long enough for a conscious choice.

MIND BEND
Choice can enter through posture before the mind has finished arguing with the impulse.

FORMULA FLOW
Identify Motor → Choose Safe → Enter Posture → Decide Consciously

SAFETY
PAUSE
Choose another response if the posture causes pain, strain, or social risk.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE FIRST DRIFT
name: THE FIRST DRIFT
goal: Catch the earliest drift before the full unwanted behaviour begins.
steps:
1. Trace the unwanted behaviour backward in your mind: first act, private permission, routine change, environment shift, body state.
2. Place a red dot on the earliest sign you could realistically notice.
3. Attach one simple interruption to that red dot and rehearse what you will do when it appears.

title: RIDE THE CRAVING GRAPH
name: RIDE THE CRAVING GRAPH
goal: Watch a craving as a changing curve before deciding what protects the next hour.
steps:
1. Notice its current level and where it moves in the body.
2. Watch for slope: rising, flattening, cresting, falling.
3. Every thirty seconds, imagine the next point without acting on the urge.
4. When the line changes direction, name the change.
5. Choose what protects the next hour.

title: COOL THE ALARM PANEL
name: COOL THE ALARM PANEL
goal: Use brief comfortable coolness as a reset cue, not a toughness test.
steps:
1. Use cool—not painfully cold—water or a wrapped cool pack on the cheeks and around the eyes for a brief interval.
2. Slow your body while the sensation lands.
3. Remove it, name the room, and reassess the next safe action.
4. Treat the cool sensation as a reset cue. Stop before it becomes an endurance test.

title: BURN THE EXCESS CHARGE

goal: Give excess body energy a safe outlet without chasing exhaustion.
steps:

3. Stop, feel the after-pulse, and let breathing settle naturally.
4. Let the body spend energy without spending your future.

title: STAY FOR THE UPDATE
name: STAY FOR THE UPDATE
goal: Stay with a manageable fear cue long enough to notice reality contradict one prediction.
steps:
1. Choose an external cue low enough on your fear ladder to approach voluntarily.
2. Enter without escape and remain until you observe at least one mismatch between prediction and reality.
3. Name the mismatch before leaving.
4. Repeat later under safe conditions rather than chasing maximum distress.

title: PUT THE DATE BACK IN
name: PUT THE DATE BACK IN
goal: Separate a memory alarm from the current moment using only present-day facts.
steps:
1. With both eyes open, state the calendar date and say where you are.
2. Name three ordinary objects you can see without describing the memory.
3. Press both feet down and point toward the nearest safe exit.
4. Say, ‘That was then; I am here now,’ then choose one neutral task.
numberedSteps:
1. With both eyes open, state the calendar date and say where you are.
2. Name three ordinary objects you can see without describing the memory.
3. Press both feet down and point toward the nearest safe exit.

numbered_steps:
1. With both eyes open, state the calendar date and say where you are.

3. Press both feet down and point toward the nearest safe exit.
4. Say, ‘That was then; I am here now,’ then choose one neutral task.
win: Those present-day cues made it easier to find where you are now and choose what comes next.
mindBend: A memory alarm can feel current without being current. Time, place, and action cues give the brain a present-tense timestamp.
mind_bend: A memory alarm can feel current without being current. Time, place, and action cues give the brain a present-tense timestamp.

3. Carry the unanswered card while doing normal life.
4. At review, notice what the urge did—not whether certainty arrived.

title: STAY THROUGH RECOVERY
name: STAY THROUGH RECOVERY
goal: Remain with a safe practice cue through the first signs of recovery, then end deliberately.
steps:
1. During a safe practice round, notice the highest point and the first downward shift.
2. Do not leave at that first relief.
3. Remain with the cue through a visible recovery phase—steady gaze, slower movement, reduced urge—then end on purpose.
4. Departure follows learning, not panic.

title: MOVE THE LESSON
name: MOVE THE LESSON
goal: Carry a learned skill into changing conditions instead of trusting it only in one setting.
steps:
1. Repeat a mastered practice while changing one feature: location, time, cue order, duration, or intensity.
2. On the next round, alter a different feature.
3. Keep a small mental map of where the skill still works.
4. Let variation turn a local success into portable knowledge.

GOAL
Carry a learned skill into changing conditions instead of trusting it only in one setting.

title: TURN UP THE WHISPER
name: TURN UP THE WHISPER
goal: Amplify one tiny spontaneous body tendency just enough to learn what it is asking for.
steps:
1. Notice the smallest spontaneous tendency: sway, curl, stretch, turn, reach.
2. Enlarge it by only ten percent and pause.
3. Check if it brings ease, protection, energy, or nothing.
4. Let the answer determine whether to continue, reverse, or stop.

title: DATE-STAMP THE PRESENT
name: DATE-STAMP THE PRESENT
goal: Anchor to today's date using the room, an exit, and reachable support.
steps:
1. Say today's full date and your current location aloud.
2. Read the names of three ordinary objects directly in front of you.
3. Point to the nearest safe exit without moving toward the past memory.
4. Name one person or service available in the present.
5. Keep eyes open and return attention to the whole room.

plain:
DATE-STAMP THE PRESENT

PLAY TIME
60–90 seconds

GOAL
Anchor to today's date using the room, an exit, and reachable support.

STEPS
1. Say today's full date and your current location aloud.
2. Read the names of three ordinary objects directly in front of you.
3. Point to the nearest safe exit without moving toward the past memory.
4. Name one person or service available in the present.
5. Keep eyes open and return attention to the whole room.

WIN
Today's date, current location, ordinary objects, a safe exit, and a present-day helper all became explicit.

Trauma memory can erase timestamps. Ordinary present facts act like metadata the alarm response did not carry with it.

goal: Feel fear as raw body sensation without letting prediction turn it into a movie.

title: STUDY THE REACTION, NOT THE CHARACTER
name: STUDY THE REACTION, NOT THE CHARACTER
ritual_name: STUDY THE REACTION, NOT THE CHARACTER
goal: Study a repeated reaction as a pattern, not as proof of your character.
steps:
1. Choose a reaction that happens often and remember three times it happened.
2. For each time, notice the trigger, meaning, body feeling, action, and result.
3. Compare the three examples with a trusted idea or guide.
4. Choose one idea to test. Leave your whole character out of the experiment.

title: WHAT REMAINS WHEN REWARD LEAVES?
name: WHAT REMAINS WHEN REWARD LEAVES?
goal: Find the responsibility that remains even when reward, praise, and punishment disappear.
steps:
1. Name your role, the people affected, and the values governing it.
2. Mentally remove applause, punishment, and personal advantage.
3. Ask which responsibility still stands.
4. Convert that answer into a time-bound action and one limit on what the role does not require.
numberedSteps:
1. Name your role, the people affected, and the values governing it.
2. Mentally remove applause, punishment, and personal advantage.
3. Ask which responsibility still stands.
4. Convert that answer into a time-bound action and one limit on what the role does not require.
numbered_steps:
1. Name your role, the people affected, and the values governing it.
2. Mentally remove applause, punishment, and personal advantage.
3. Ask which responsibility still stands.
4. Convert that answer into a time-bound action and one limit on what the role does not require.
win: One value-based duty survived the removal of personal advantage and became a time-bound action with a clear limit.
mindBend: A responsibility that vanishes without applause may have been serving reward more than values. What remains reveals the deeper contract.

goal: Move anger or alarm through controlled physical effort without rehearsing harm.
steps:

full_consumer_ritual:
PLAY TIME
about 1 minute

GOAL
Move anger or alarm through controlled physical effort without rehearsing harm.

STEPS
1. Choose shaking, wall-free pushing motions, stamping, stretching, or strong walking.
2. Decide a safe maximum intensity and ten controlled repetitions.
3. Complete the repetitions without rehearsing violence.
4. Stand still afterward until you notice the earliest easing signal.

WIN
The chosen repetitions stayed within a safe limit and ended at the first detectable easing signal.

MIND BEND
Physical charge can be discharged without giving violent imagery a rehearsal session alongside it.

FORMULA FLOW
Choose Release → Set Limit → Move → Find Settling

SAFETY
PAUSE
Stop for pain, dizziness, aggression, or loss of action control.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BREAK THE DEADLINE MONOLITH
name: BREAK THE DEADLINE MONOLITH
goal: Turn one looming deadline into separate usable work blocks with visible finishes.
steps:
1. Count the usable work blocks remaining, subtracting sleep and fixed duties.
2. Give each block one deliverable with a visible finish.
3. Place buffers before the final deadline.
4. Start the earliest window; refuse to mentally carry later windows inside it.

name: TWENTY SECONDS BEFORE THE STORY
goal: Describe the body's physics before choosing an emotion label or story.
steps:
1. For twenty seconds, ban emotion names and causes.
2. Say only geometry and physics: shape, temperature, pressure, texture, direction, pulse.
3. At the bell, choose the smallest plain word that fits, or keep it unnamed if none does.

title: NO-CONCEPT MINUTE
name: NO-CONCEPT MINUTE
goal: Spend one minute with direct sensation before concepts are allowed to explain it.
steps:
1. Set a brief interval.
2. During it, do not create causes, labels, comparisons, or solutions.
3. Attend to direct colour, sound, contact, and movement.
4. If a concept appears, acknowledge ‘explanation’ and let the sensory world continue.

title: THE EMOTION STOPS AT THE SKIN
name: THE EMOTION STOPS AT THE SKIN
ritual_name: THE EMOTION STOPS AT THE SKIN
goal: Keep another person's emotion on their side of the boundary while choosing what help is truly yours.
steps:
1. Notice where their emotion seems to enter your body.
2. Trace your physical boundary with gaze or touch.
3. State what action is yours, what remains theirs, and what you can offer without taking ownership.
4. Adjust distance if the distinction stays blurred.

name: ASK WHAT THE MEMORY IS STILL BILLING
ritual_name: ASK WHAT THE MEMORY IS STILL BILLING
goal: Find what a memory is still demanding and route that demand to the right present response.
steps:

4. Choose the matching present response: set protection, request safe repair, make room for grief, or stop billing today for a reversal history cannot provide.

full_consumer_ritual:
PLAY TIME
45–60 seconds

GOAL
Prepare the exact recovery sequence for the first lapse before a second lapse can be negotiated.

STEPS
1. Pre-plan three actions after a lapse: name what happened without judgement; restore the environment or schedule; do the next smallest valid repetition.
2. Store the script beside the behaviour.
3. Use it after one miss—before a second is negotiated.

WIN
One miss triggered naming, restoration, and the next valid repetition without a character judgment.

MIND BEND
A lapse becomes a pattern partly through the story and delay that follow it; rehearsed recovery shortens the gap before the next good repetition.

FORMULA FLOW
Name Event → Store → Use After

SAFETY
PAUSE
Escalate to support when lapses involve danger, relapse, or repeated loss of control.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE UNANSWERED URGE EXPERIMENT
name: THE UNANSWERED URGE EXPERIMENT
goal: Delay one answer-seeking urge and watch whether the need for information survives the wait.
steps:
1. When the question demands an answer, picture it and delay asking for a short, chosen interval.
2. Track urge intensity at beginning, middle, and end without researching.
3. Decide afterward whether information is still needed for action or only for relief.

full_consumer_ritual:
PLAY TIME
45–60 seconds

GOAL
Give extra thinking time only to topics that can name both a question and a useful result.

STEPS
1. Before giving a topic more time, name the exact question and the useful result you need: decision, plan, explanation, message, or acceptance.
2. If either is missing, deny the session and return to direct life.

WIN
A thought without a clear question or deliverable lost its meeting time and attention returned to direct life.

MIND BEND
Thinking feels productive by default. Requiring an agenda reveals how often the mind is holding meetings with no decision on the agenda.

FORMULA FLOW
Give Topic → Return Direct

SAFETY
PAUSE
Allow free reflection and creativity when productivity is not the purpose.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: NOTICE THE SPACE DOING THE HOLDING
name: NOTICE THE SPACE DOING THE HOLDING
ritual_name: NOTICE THE SPACE DOING THE HOLDING
goal: Make the empty space around and between things as noticeable as the things themselves.
steps:

3. Reverse figure and ground until space feels as noticeable as matter.
4. Include the sense of room around your body.

title: LET THE WATCHER GO TOO
name: LET THE WATCHER GO TOO
goal: Notice the feeling of being ‘the watcher’ without having to keep that position in place.
steps:
1. Notice the subtle feeling that says ‘I am the observer’.
2. Treat that feeling or location as another experience you can notice.
3. Let awareness continue without holding a separate watcher in place.
4. Return to an ordinary action straight afterward.

steps:

3. Notice what changes inside as the symbol changes.
4. Turn that inner shift into one practical next move.

full_consumer_ritual:
PLAY TIME
60–120 seconds

GOAL
Keep one work thread active and save its resume point before another switch can take over.

STEPS
1. Mentally name the exact restart instruction.
2. Let the urge to keep switching weaken slightly.
3. Mute one distraction that competes with the work lane.
4. Say one usable first line aloud.
5. Settle on the resume point you will return to.

WIN
One distraction was muted, a usable opening line appeared, and the active thread ended with a clear return marker.

MIND BEND
Working memory is easier to protect by reducing simultaneous threads than by trying to hold every thread more tightly.

FORMULA FLOW
Store Handoff → Stop Clean → Block Noise → Open It → Set Bookmark

PAUSE

goal: Lower the threat level of the exchange without weakening the actual question.
steps:
1. Notice the exact tone cue that made the exchange feel unsafe.

3. Ask for one concrete form of help or clarification.

full_consumer_ritual:
PLAY TIME
45–90 seconds

GOAL
End repeated body checking and bring another person into the situation.

STEPS
1. Name one plain fact about what you are checking in your body.
2. Loosen the urge to check again.
3. Call someone safe or move toward them.

WIN
One factual check was enough; the next move was toward a safe person rather than back toward the body.

MIND BEND
Checking promises certainty but often teaches attention that the body must be watched. Stopping after one fact breaks that training loop.

FORMULA FLOW
Name Place → Catch Thought → Reach Person

SAFETY
PAUSE
Keep your eyes open and orient to the room. Stop if symptoms intensify, you feel faint, or a medical problem may be possible. Call Triple Zero (000) for an emergency; otherwise use qualified medical advice. Do not induce or test symptoms.
This is brief self-help, not diagnosis or treatment.

PLAY TIME
60–120 seconds

GOAL
Break past rehearsal by separating the situation from self-judgment and allowing another view to enter.

STEPS
1. Name one brief holding cue.
2. Separate the situation from the self-judgment.
3. Name one visible change.
4. Complete the smallest next move.
5. Name one unfinished loop.

WIN
One visible change led to the smallest next move while the unfinished loop was named rather than reopened.

MIND BEND
Self-judgment makes a past event feel closed to new interpretation. Once identity is removed from the evidence, another view can actually fit.

FORMULA FLOW
Make Cue → Unmix Story → Park Rest → Begin Now → Open Loop

PAUSE

name: LEAVE THE DOOR OPEN
goal: Stop fighting the thought and continue one small task without checking whether it left.
steps:
1. Say, “This thought is allowed to be here for this minute.”
2. Notice one sound or object outside your head without using it to escape or prove anything.
3. Start one small task while letting the thought remain in the background.
4. Do not check whether the thought has faded before continuing.
